traveler: Abu Sa'id 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ghafiqi
title: The Pavement of the Martyrs: the Wali of al-Andalus, the Road to Tours, and the Field Nobody Can Find
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Tihama and the Road West

stops.name: Tihama, born to the tribe of Ghafiq
stops.date_confidence: No birth year survives in any source. 'Late seventh century' is inferred backwards from his seniority in 721. The birthplace is contested: English Wikipedia gives Tihamah and calls Ghafiq a Tihamite tribe; Arabic Wikipedia gives the Hijaz, some 800 km north. The pin follows the Tihamite reading and the conflict is not resolved.
stops.campa: He is born into the Ghafiq, a tribe reckoned to the 'Akk, and the sources cannot agree where. One tradition sets the cradle in the Tihama, the hot coastal shelf along the Red Sea. The other sets it in the Hijaz, eight hundred kilometres north. No chronicler gives a town and none gives a year. The name comes down entire where the birthplace does not: Abu Sa'id 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Bishr ibn al-Sarim al-Ghafiqi. The record picks him up only when he is already a grown man in the Maghreb, with a career behind him that nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The Tihama coastal plain and the tribal geography of the 'Akk

stops.name: Kairouan, the province that made him
stops.date_confidence: Undated in every source. Later biography places him in this milieu without giving a year; the date shown is a placeholder for 'early eighth century'.
stops.campa: Ifriqiya is governed from Kairouan, and the later biographers put him in that circle: known to Musa ibn Nusayr, who took al-Andalus, and to Musa's son 'Abd al-Aziz. The province exists because the same Umayyad advance had broken Dihya in the Aures a generation earlier and sent her head east to Damascus as proof of it. Kairouan is where commissions for the far west are written. His own second commission will be written here thirty years from now, by a governor whose name the later accounts will get wrong. Nothing fixes how long he stays.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Kairouan and the Umayyad administration of Ifriqiya

stops.name: Ceuta, the crossing of the strait
stops.date_confidence: Not recorded anywhere. The crossing is read backwards from his presence in the peninsula by 721; the year shown is an inference from the governorate of 'Abd al-Aziz ibn Musa and nothing firmer.
stops.campa: Somewhere in these years he crosses the narrows that Tariq ibn Ziyad opened in 711, by Ceuta and the ferry road the conquest armies used. No chronicle records the crossing. It is read backwards from his presence in the peninsula in 721, already senior enough to hold a command under the wali and to be named when the wali dies. Nine miles of water separate two of his lives: the tribesman out of Arabia by way of Ifriqiya, and the officer of a province four years old that has not yet decided where its own capital sits.
suggested_refs: The Strait of Gibraltar and the 711 crossing route from Ceuta

stops.name: Seville, the seat already moved
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No source names Seville as his post; the connection is his reported acquaintance with 'Abd al-Aziz ibn Musa, whose capital it had been. The month is arbitrary.
stops.campa: He enters al-Andalus while the memory of 'Abd al-Aziz ibn Musa is fresh and Seville is still spoken of as the head of the province. It is no longer the head. Al-Hurr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Thaqafi, governor from 716, moves the administration to Cordoba soon after taking office, and the move is finished before al-Samh arrives in 719. No source names Seville as al-Ghafiqi's post. The connection is one reported acquaintance and nothing else, which is the whole documentary basis of his first thirty-five years.
suggested_refs: Seville as the first Umayyad capital of al-Andalus, before the transfer to Cordoba
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Al-Hurr ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Thaqafi'
English Wikipedia, 'List of Umayyad governors of al-Andalus'

stops.name: Cordoba, the seat of the wali
stops.date_confidence: Al-Samh's governorship from March 719 is attested in the governors list. Al-Ghafiqi's service under him is attested in the biography without dates or duties.
stops.campa: The province is governed from Cordoba on the Guadalquivir, and al-Samh ibn Malik al-Khawlani holds it from March of 719. Al-Ghafiqi serves under him; what he does is not written down. The city will keep the seat through both his own terms and long past them. A century from now Ziryab will bring the lute to these streets. Ibn Rushd will receive the young Ibn Arabi inside these walls, and Maimonides will be born a few streets from the mosque four hundred years on. For the moment it is a garrison town administering a conquest that has not stopped moving north.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad governor's palace and the mosque quarter of Cordoba
sources: English Wikipedia, 'List of Umayyad governors of al-Andalus'

stops.name: Narbonne, the forward base in Gaul
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The capture of Narbonne in the campaign begun in 719 is attested; no source says the Toulouse army mustered there or advanced from there. The muster is inferred from Narbonne being the only Umayyad city north of the Pyrenees.
stops.campa: Narbonne fell in the campaign begun in 719 and is the one city the Umayyads hold north of the Pyrenees. Al-Samh assembles an army of Arabs and Berbers and turns it inland toward Aquitaine. The chronicles do not say the muster happened in Narbonne; they say the city was taken first and the war went on from there, which is how a forward base gets inferred. Al-Ghafiqi marches with this force. It is the first campaign any source places him in, and he is forty or so, and unnamed until it goes wrong.
suggested_refs: Narbonne, Umayyad since 719, the base of every campaign into Gaul

stops.name: Toulouse, the siege broken by Odo
stops.date_confidence: attested; 9 June 721 per English Wikipedia, 'Battle of Toulouse (721)'
stops.campa: Duke Odo of Aquitaine comes down on the siege lines before Toulouse and breaks them. Al-Samh is mortally wounded and dies trying to withdraw. The army scatters south through country it had ridden through as conquerors three months before. Among the officers who get clear is 'Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, and this is the first time the sources give his name at all. Two hundred and thirteen years ago Clovis came to this same city and carried off the treasure of Alaric. Odo has done what nobody in Gaul has managed since 711: stopped an Umayyad army in the field.
suggested_refs: The siege lines before Toulouse, 721, and Odo's relieving march

stops.name: Narbonne, the survivors fall back
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction from the biography; the retreat route and its timing are not given in the sources.
stops.campa: The wreck of the army comes back over the passes to Narbonne, which is all that is left of the position north of the mountains. Al-Ghafiqi is left holding the eastern reaches, the frontier the disaster has opened. Toulouse has cost the province a governor and a field army in a single afternoon. The Latin annals will remember it; the Arabic tradition will spend the next four centuries not writing about it, in the same silence it will later keep about the larger defeat that ends his life eleven years from now.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad frontier command in eastern al-Andalus after Toulouse

stops.name: Cordoba, elected wali by the army
stops.date_confidence: Contested length. Arabic Wikipedia gives Dhu al-Hijjah 102 to Safar 103 AH, converting to 6 June to 1 September 721. The English governors list gives July 721 alone, with 'Anbasa from August. The English biography infobox says 721-722, a full year, and is the outlier. Not resolved.
stops.campa: With al-Samh dead the army in the field elects its own governor and chooses him. The term is measured in weeks: Dhu al-Hijjah of 102 to Safar of 103, the sixth of June to the first of September. The governors' list gives him July and nothing more. His own biography stretches it to a year, and the two cannot both be true. Nothing at all is recorded of what he did with the office. Kairouan sends 'Anbasa ibn Suhaym al-Kalbi, and he hands it over. It is the only command in his life given to him by soldiers rather than by a province.
suggested_refs: The list of Umayyad governors of al-Andalus and its disagreement with the biographies
sources: English Wikipedia, 'List of Umayyad governors of al-Andalus'

stops.name: Cordoba, 'Anbasa takes the seat
stops.date_confidence: attested; 'Anbasa's tenure August 721 to January 726 per the governors list
stops.campa: 'Anbasa ibn Suhaym al-Kalbi governs from August of 721 and carries the frontier war back north into Gaul, where he will die campaigning in January of 726. For the whole of that governorship al-Ghafiqi is absent from the chronicles. 'Anbasa's tenure is dated to the month; the officers who rode under him are not named at all. He is somewhere on the eastern march, in a command the sources describe by inference and never once name, and four and a half years pass without a single dated act attached to him anywhere in Arabic or in Latin.
suggested_refs: 'Anbasa ibn Suhaym al-Kalbi's campaigns into southern Gaul, 721-726
sources: English Wikipedia, 'List of Umayyad governors of al-Andalus'

stops.name: Zaragoza, the eastern march
stops.date_confidence: Pure reconstruction. No chronicle places him in Zaragoza or anywhere else between 721 and 730. The command is inferred from his later familiarity with the Catalan passes.
stops.campa: The march running up the Ebro toward Zaragoza and the Pyrenean approaches is the province's exposed side, and it is where a soldier who came out of Toulouse alive would be kept. No chronicle puts him in the city. The command is read backwards from the shape of the later career: a man who in 731 knows the Catalan passes well enough to march into them and finish a rebellion in one season learned that country somewhere, and this is the only place he could have learned it. The years between are otherwise blank.
suggested_refs: The Upper March of al-Andalus and the Ebro frontier

stops.name: Narbonne, 'Anbasa does not come home
stops.date_confidence: attested; 'Anbasa killed campaigning in southern Gaul, January 726
stops.campa: 'Anbasa is killed campaigning in southern Gaul in January of 726, the second wali in five years to die north of the mountains. Narbonne holds. What does not hold is the government. The seat passes to 'Udhra ibn 'Abd Allah al-Fihri inside the month, and from him to a line of men appointed out of Kairouan who arrive, sit, and are replaced before their orders can reach the frontier. The war into Gaul stops for four years, not because the Franks stop it but because there is nobody in Cordoba long enough to order it on.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad position in Septimania after 'Anbasa's death
sources: English Wikipedia, 'List of Umayyad governors of al-Andalus'

stops.name: Cordoba, six governors in four years
stops.date_confidence: attested; all six tenures dated in the governors list, January 726 to March 730
stops.campa: Between January of 726 and March of 730 six men hold the province: 'Udhra ibn 'Abd Allah al-Fihri, Yahya ibn Salama al-Kalbi, Hudhayfa ibn al-Ahwas al-Ashja'i, 'Uthman ibn Abi Nis'a al-Khath'ami, al-Haytham ibn 'Ubayd al-Kilabi, Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ashja'i. Not one lasts two years and two of them last four months. Every one is sent from Ifriqiya. Underneath the turnover the Mudari and the Yamani, the Arabs of the north and the Arabs of the south, are dividing the army against itself.
suggested_refs: The governor list of al-Andalus, 726-730, and the Mudari-Yamani split
sources: English Wikipedia, 'List of Umayyad governors of al-Andalus'

stops.name: Kairouan, the commission sent west
stops.date_confidence: March 730 per the governors list. Arabic Wikipedia dates the term from Safar 113 AH, which converts to 18 April to 16 May 731, a full year later. The two datings do not agree and are not reconciled by any source.
stops.campa: The commission for the seventh governor in nine years goes out from Kairouan. The man who signs it is 'Ubayda ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, governor of Ifriqiya since 727. Later accounts name 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Habhab instead, who will not hold Kairouan until 734, two years after al-Ghafiqi is dead; the two names are close enough that somebody swapped them and everyone since has copied it. The Arabic biography puts the commission in Safar of 113, which falls in the spring of 731, a full year after the lists put him in the seat.
suggested_refs: The Ifriqiyan chancery at Kairouan and its appointments to al-Andalus
sources: English Wikipedia, 'List of Umayyad governors of al-Andalus'

stops.name: Damascus, the caliph in whose name he governs
stops.date_confidence: Hisham's caliphate from 724 is attested. The claim that Hisham personally appointed al-Ghafiqi is not supported by either the English or the Arabic biography; on the evidence the appointment came from Ifriqiya. Tagged as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Al-Andalus is a march of a march: governed from Cordoba under Kairouan under Damascus, where Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik has sat as caliph since 724. Some accounts have Hisham naming him with his own hand. Neither biography says so, and the commission on the evidence comes from Ifriqiya. Damascus is where the head of Dihya was carried as proof that the Aures had been broken, and where the news from the Garonne will arrive so late and so thin that the chroniclers there will file it under skirmishes. It is four thousand miles from the field he dies on.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad caliphal court of Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik at Damascus and Rusafa

stops.name: Cordoba, wali a second time
stops.date_confidence: March 730 per the governors list; the Arabic tradition's Safar 113 AH points to spring 731. The reconciliation of Mudari and Yamani rests on Arabic Wikipedia alone and is tagged as reconstruction.
stops.campa: He takes the seat in March and spends the first stretch of it on the quarrel eating the army from inside: Mudari against Yamani, the northern Arabs against the southern, a feud carried whole out of Arabia and set down on the Guadalquivir. The Arabic biography credits him with reconciling them, and no other source mentions it. He will need them riding in one column inside eighteen months. The city he governs from will hold Ziryab's lute in a century and Maimonides' cradle in four.
suggested_refs: The Mudari and Yamani factions in the army of al-Andalus

stops.name: Cerdanya, the marriage that made a lordship
stops.date_confidence: attested for 730 per English Wikipedia, 'Uthman ibn Naissa'; the month is not given
stops.campa: 'Uthman ibn Naissa, whom the Latin sources call Munuza, is the Berber deputy holding the Cerdanya and the Catalan Pyrenees. In 730 he makes peace with Odo of Aquitaine and marries Odo's daughter Lampegia, and the raiding into Aquitaine stops. For a season there is a lordship in the mountains answering to neither Cordoba nor Toulouse, held together by one marriage. Berbers took most of the peninsula for the Umayyads and were given the worst of it to garrison. Munuza is what that arrangement produces when it is left alone long enough.
suggested_refs: The Cerdanya marches and the Berber garrisons of the Pyrenean frontier

stops.name: Llivia, the revolt put down
stops.date_confidence: The revolt and its suppression are attested for c. 731; the month is not given. Llivia is the traditional site and is flagged as unconfirmed in the source itself. The biography says al-Ghafiqi killed Munuza; the article on Munuza says he was defeated in battle and executed.
stops.campa: Munuza renounces Cordoba, kills Nambaudus the bishop of Urgell, and tries to make a mountain lordship into a state. Al-Ghafiqi marches into the Cerdanya and ends it in one campaign. One account says he killed him; another says Munuza was beaten in the field and executed after. Lampegia is taken and sent east to the caliph. The traditional site of the last stand is Llivia, which the sources decline to confirm. Odo, who gave his daughter to a man who then rebelled, is now a duke with a case to answer.
suggested_refs: Llivia in the Cerdanya, traditional site of Munuza's last stand

stops.name: Cordoba, the province called to arms
stops.date_confidence: The accusation against Odo as pretext is reconstruction. The call for volunteers from Yemen and the Levant is flagged dubious in the English Wikipedia article itself and must stay a reconstruction; the month is arbitrary.
stops.campa: He puts the charge to Odo in public: that Aquitaine armed the revolt. The pretext for the largest expedition the Umayyads will ever send north of the Pyrenees is a father-in-law. The biography says he called for volunteers out of Yemen and the Levant to come to Cordoba for it, and then flags its own sentence as doubtful; no chronicle carries the summons. What is certain is narrower: a province that had six governors in four years produces one army, under one man, in one season.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad summons of 731 and its doubtful attestation

stops.name: Pamplona, the host assembled
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No source names an assembly point; the sources say only that the force crossed the Pyrenees at their western end, through Navarre. The month is inferred from a summer campaign.
stops.campa: The army goes north through Navarre, and the tradition has it gather at Pamplona before the passes. No chronicle names an assembly point. What the sources say is only that the force crossed the Pyrenees at their western end. Medieval writers put seventy or eighty thousand men in it, a figure Matthew Bennett repeats and modern historians reject on the ground that no eighth-century commander could feed them; the sober estimates run fifteen to thirty thousand. Forty-six years from now Charlemagne will have this city's gates opened to him and pull its walls down on the way home.
suggested_refs: Matthew Bennett, The Hutchinson Dictionary of Ancient and Medieval Warfare (1998), on the chronicle figures
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Battle of the River Garonne'

stops.name: Roncesvalles, over the Pyrenees
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No source names the pass; Roncevaux is chosen as the customary road between Pamplona and Aquitaine. The month is inferred.
stops.campa: The column takes the western defile, by custom the road between Pamplona and Aquitaine. No source names the pass; the geography names it for them. In 778 Charlemagne's rearguard will die in this same throat of rock, and be sung about for four hundred years afterwards, and the singers will make the killers Saracens because this is the pass the Saracens came through. Below it the country is Gascon, thinly held, and open all the way to the Garonne. Nobody in Aquitaine has yet been told that the army is on the road.
suggested_refs: The Roncevaux pass, crossed in 732 and again in 778

stops.name: Bayonne, the ride through Vasconia
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The raiding through Vasconia toward Bordeaux is attested; Bayonne itself is named in no account and stands here for the region's chief town on that road. The date is a route estimate.
stops.campa: They come down into Vasconia and go through it taking what they pass. Bayonne is the region's chief town on that road, and neither it nor anything else is named in the accounts: what survives is a record of plunder along a march, without places attached. The Gascon country does not resist and is not asked to. Odo has one field army left and it is at Bordeaux, four days north. He has beaten an Umayyad army once, eleven years ago at Toulouse, and the man riding at him now was standing in it when it broke.
stops.quote: And that army went through all places like a desolating storm. Prosperity made those warriors insatiable.
stops.quote_source: Arabic chroniclers as rendered by Jose Antonio Conde, Historia de la Dominacion de los Arabes en Espana (1820), quoted in Edward Shepherd Creasy, The Fifteen Decisive Battles of the World, ch. VII
suggested_refs: Creasy's chapter VII and its Conde-derived Saracenic narrative
sources: Wikisource, Creasy, The Fifteen Decisive Battles of the World, ch. VII

stops.name: Bordeaux, the city taken
stops.date_confidence: The defeat of Odo before the city and the sack are attested for 732; no source gives a day or a month. The date shown is a campaign estimate.
stops.campa: Odo gathers his army at Bordeaux and is beaten outside the walls, and the city is sacked. Two hundred and twenty-five years ago Clovis wintered here after Vouille, having taken Aquitaine off the Goths in one campaigning season: the same river, the same argument about who holds the south. The Arabic sources call the city al-Burdhil, which later writers will mistake for the name of a battle. The plunder taken here will be loaded into wagons and dragged north, and it will decide the war.
suggested_refs: Bordeaux in 732, sacked between Odo's two defeats
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Battle of the River Garonne'

stops.name: Bordeaux, the basilica of Saint-Seurin
stops.date_confidence: The site is of this antiquity; the standing building is not. Nave and choir are 11th to 13th century, the south portal 13th, chapels 14th to 15th. A 5th-century oratory on the site had disappeared by the 9th century. Only 4th-century palaeochristian necropolis remains in the crypt predate the raid.
stops.campa: Outside the walls stands the burial ground of Saint-Seurin, old already, a Christian necropolis since the fourth century and an oratory over it since the fifth. The church that stands there now was built afterwards, stone by stone, from the eleventh century to the fifteenth, so that nothing above ground at Saint-Seurin is anything al-Ghafiqi's men could have seen. What they saw is under the present floor. Isidore of Beja, writing twenty-two years later, says only that they destroyed palaces and burned churches, and names none of them.
suggested_refs: The palaeochristian necropolis in the crypt of Saint-Seurin, Bordeaux
sources: Fordham Medieval Sourcebook, 'Arabs, Franks, and the Battle of Tours, 732'

stops.name: The Garonne, Odo's second army destroyed
stops.date_confidence: The battle is attested for 732 without a day. The coordinate is English Wikipedia's, at the Garonne and Dordogne confluence near the Bec d'Ambes, which is why the article hedges 'or possibly at the Dordogne'.
stops.campa: On the Garonne, or on the Dordogne as one account has it, the cavalry destroys what is left of Odo's field army. The chronicler will not put a number on the dead and says so. The defeat is total. Odo himself gets clear and rides north to beg help from Charles Martel, mayor of the palace of the Franks, the one man in Gaul with an army that has not yet been broken this year, and the one man Odo has spent his whole career keeping out of Aquitaine. Aquitaine now has no field army at all.
stops.quote: He gave battle to Duke Eudes (of Aquitaine) beyond the Garonne and the Dordogne, and put him to flight---so utterly [was he beaten] that God alone knew the number of the slain and wounded.
stops.quote_source: Isidore of Beja, the Mozarabic Chronicle of 754, in Davis, Readings in Ancient History, vol. II, pp. 362-364; Fordham Medieval Sourcebook, 'Arabs, Franks, and the Battle of Tours, 732'
suggested_refs: The Bec d'Ambes and the Garonne-Dordogne confluence, the located site of the 732 battle
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Battle of the River Garonne'
Fordham Medieval Sourcebook, 'Arabs, Franks, and the Battle of Tours, 732'

stops.name: Angouleme, the road north
stops.date_confidence: Route inference only. No source places the army at Angouleme; the itinerary between the Garonne and Poitiers is reconstructed from geography and is not attested at any point.
stops.campa: The march north from the Garonne runs, by the likeliest road, through Angouleme. No source confirms the army passing the town, and no source names any other town on the stretch either. The whole itinerary between the Garonne and Poitiers is reconstructed from roads and river crossings rather than from anything anyone wrote. Behind the column the wagons come slower every week, heavier every week, and by the time the Franks are found the army is strung out along a hundred miles of Aquitaine.
suggested_refs: The Roman road from Burdigala to Limonum, the likely line of advance

segments.name: The Road Between Poitiers and Tours

stops.name: Poitiers, the basilica of Saint-Hilaire
stops.date_confidence: General devastation on the approach is attested; the specific tradition that Saint-Hilaire was burned or threatened is later tradition and is not in the near-contemporary chronicles. The date is an estimate.
stops.campa: The army devastates southern Gaul on its approach to Poitiers. Later tradition, not the earliest chronicles, credits the church of Saint-Hilaire with being burned or threatened in the raiding; the near-contemporary sources describe the destruction in general terms and name no building. It is the pattern of this campaign: the closer a detail comes to a place a visitor can stand in, the later the source that carries it, and the more confidently it gets repeated.
suggested_refs: Saint-Hilaire-le-Grand at Poitiers and the later traditions of its burning

stops.name: Tours, the shrine of Saint Martin named as the prize
stops.date_confidence: The abbey of Saint Martin as the campaign's objective is attested in English Wikipedia, 'Battle of Tours'. The date is the conventional reading of the approach and is not itself given in the sources.
stops.campa: The wealth of the abbey of Saint Martin at Tours is named as the target, and it draws the army past Poitiers and north toward the Loire, ahead of its own wagons and a good part of its own strength. He never reaches it. Clovis heard the psalm sung in this church in 507 and took it for an omen. Charles Martel will give thanks here in November. Seven hundred years from now a girl from Domremy will be armed in this town, and the sword she asks for will be dug out of a church floor thirty miles south.
stops.quote: Whereupon Abderrahman set in pursuit of Eudes; he destroyed palaces, burned churches, and imagined he could pillage the basilica of St. Martin of Tours.
stops.quote_source: Isidore of Beja, the Mozarabic Chronicle of 754; Fordham Medieval Sourcebook, 'Arabs, Franks, and the Battle of Tours, 732'
suggested_refs: The basilica and treasury of Saint Martin at Tours, named objective of the 732 campaign
sources: Fordham Medieval Sourcebook, 'Arabs, Franks, and the Battle of Tours, 732'

stops.name: The confluence of the Clain and the Vienne
stops.date_confidence: The confluence is at Cenon-sur-Vienne, just south of Chatellerault, per French Wikipedia. That the battle was fought near it is a modern reconstruction, not a fix given by the chroniclers; French Wikipedia counts no fewer than thirty-eight proposed sites.
stops.campa: The Clain comes down out of Poitiers and joins the Vienne at Cenon, below Chatellerault, and modern accounts fix the battlefield by that junction because no town or fortress gives the field a name of its own. The chroniclers do not fix it there. They do not fix it anywhere. French scholarship counts thirty-eight proposed sites for the battle and declines to choose between them, which leaves the engagement the nineteenth century called decisive floating loose over a hundred square miles of Poitou.
suggested_refs: The Clain-Vienne confluence at Cenon-sur-Vienne, and the thirty-eight candidate battlefields

stops.name: Moussais, seven days of watching
stops.date_confidence: The seven days of skirmishing before full engagement are attested in English Wikipedia, 'Battle of Tours'. The Moussais location is one reconstruction among thirty-eight; French Wikipedia says only that it is possible the battle took place on this commune.
stops.campa: Charles Martel intercepts the invasion near the hamlet of Moussais, on high wooded ground he has picked himself, and refuses to come down off it. For seven days the two armies skirmish without closing, each recalling its raiding parties, each waiting for the other to be stupid first. Martel has walked his infantry across Gaul to be here and has no cavalry worth the name. Al-Ghafiqi has cavalry and a hundred miles of loot behind him. Whoever moves first must come uphill into the other.
suggested_refs: The Moussais-la-Bataille interpretive site at Vouneuil-sur-Vienne

stops.name: The field, the wall of ice
stops.date_confidence: Four datings, unreconciled. English Wikipedia: 10 October 732. French Wikipedia, 'Vouneuil-sur-Vienne': 25 October 732. Arabic Wikipedia: 27 Sha'ban 114 AH, which converts to 26 October 732, not the 21 October the source prints. French Wikipedia, 'Bataille de Poitiers (732)': 25 October 732 or 17 October 733. Two of the four converge on late October; the English date is the outlier and is used here only as an index.
stops.campa: The armies close. Umayyad cavalry goes in against Frankish infantry drawn up in a square on the slope, and for the first time in twenty years of riding into Gaul the horses do not go through. The Franks stand shoulder to shoulder and hold, and the chronicler reaching for a way to say it reaches for ice. The charges go in again and again through the day. The fighting goes on all day, which is longer than an army with a hundred miles of plunder strung out behind it can afford.
stops.quote: Firmly they stood, one close to another, forming as it were a bulwark of ice; and with great blows of their swords they hewed down the Arabs.
stops.quote_source: Isidore of Beja, the Mozarabic Chronicle of 754; Fordham Medieval Sourcebook, 'Arabs, Franks, and the Battle of Tours, 732'
suggested_refs: The Frankish infantry square of 732 and Isidore of Beja's account of it
sources: Fordham Medieval Sourcebook, 'Arabs, Franks, and the Battle of Tours, 732'

stops.name: The camp, the plunder defended
stops.date_confidence: The tactical sequence is attested in English Wikipedia, 'Battle of Tours'. The date carries the same four-way disagreement as the engagement itself.
stops.campa: Word runs through the Umayyad line that Frankish scouts are in the camp among the wagons. Part of the army turns to save what it has spent four months taking out of Aquitaine, and the line comes apart behind them, and what began as a detachment riding back becomes an army leaving. The plunder of Bordeaux, which paid for the campaign and made it worth mounting, is the thing that loses it. This is the account the sources give and it is the only tactical explanation anybody has ever offered for the collapse.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad baggage train of 732 and its part in the collapse

stops.name: The field, the death of al-Ghafiqi
stops.date_confidence: The manner of death is attested by the Mozarabic Chronicle of 754. The Arabic tradition instead has him mortally wounded by an arrow while reordering the ranks; the two accounts are not reconciled. The date carries the full four-way disagreement.
stops.campa: He rides into the collapse to stop it and is surrounded. The Chronicle of 754 has the Austrasians find him and strike him on the chest, and calls him a king, which he never was; the Latin west has no word for wali and will not acquire one. The Arabic tradition has him hit by an arrow while reordering the ranks. Both accounts stand, and neither is preferred. He is somewhere past fifty, seven weeks' ride from Cordoba and four thousand miles from wherever it was in Arabia he was born.
stops.quote: The people of Austrasia... killed the king, Abd ar-Rahman, when they found him, striking him on the chest.
stops.quote_source: The Mozarabic Chronicle of 754, as quoted in English Wikipedia, 'Battle of Tours'
suggested_refs: The Mozarabic Chronicle of 754, the only near-contemporary account of the death

stops.name: The camp abandoned in the night
stops.date_confidence: The night withdrawal is attested; the day after the engagement is inferred from it, and inherits the same disagreement over the engagement's date.
stops.campa: With their commander dead and the rival officers unable to agree on a successor, the army goes in the dark. It leaves the tents standing and most of what it took out of Aquitaine sitting in them, so that the Franks the next morning form up for a second day's battle against an empty camp. Nobody pursues. The campaign that had gone farthest north of any Umayyad campaign in the west ends without a treaty and without a name that anyone at the time bothered to give it.
suggested_refs: The abandoned Umayyad camp and the Frankish reconnaissance of the morning after

stops.name: Narbonne, the last Umayyad city in Gaul
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The retreat south over the Pyrenees is attested; that the survivors fell back through Narbonne is inference from Narbonne being the only Umayyad holding north of the mountains. The month is an estimate.
stops.campa: The survivors come south over the mountains and fall back on Narbonne, which is still the only city the Umayyads hold north of them and will stay so for another quarter-century. From here the frontier war with the Franks goes on for another generation under other commanders. Charles Martel will lay siege to this city in 737 and fail to take it, and it will hold out until 759, twenty-seven years after the field. Al-Ghafiqi does not come back with them, and no source in any language records where they left him.
suggested_refs: Narbonne, Umayyad from 719 until 759, and Martel's failed siege of 737

stops.name: Cordoba, the news of the defeat
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No source describes the arrival of the news in Cordoba or dates it; the province's return to governor-by-governor instability after 732 is attested in the governors list.
stops.campa: The news comes back down the Ebro road to a province that has just spent nine years failing to keep a governor alive in office and has now lost another one. The reconciliation of Mudari and Yamani that the Arabic biography credits to him does not outlast him. Within twenty years the factions will be at open war and the province will be ready for a fugitive prince of the house of Umayya to walk into it and take it. Nobody in Cordoba records the battle by a name. It is a defeat on a frontier, and there have been others.
suggested_refs: The governors of al-Andalus after 732 and the collapse into factional war
sources: English Wikipedia, 'List of Umayyad governors of al-Andalus'

stops.name: Louchapt, the cliff of the Sangou
stops.date_confidence: Local tradition, contradicting the mainstream account. Haut-Quercy holds that he was not killed at Poitiers but withdrew toward Narbonne and was killed in 733 at Louchapt, under the Sangou cliff. No coordinates for the Sangou site were locatable and the tradition's source base was not identified.
stops.campa: The Haut-Quercy tells it differently. In that country he is not killed at Poitiers at all: he pulls back toward Narbonne, is caught the following year at Louchapt under the cliff of the Sangou, and his army is destroyed there by a Frankish pursuit. No document supports it and no archaeology has been done on it. It survives because a region that has a cliff and a memory of Saracens will eventually put the two together, and because a commander who has no grave anywhere can be given one anywhere.
suggested_refs: The Sangou cliff at Louchapt and the Haut-Quercy tradition of a 733 death

stops.name: The road between Poitiers and Tours, balat al-shuhada
stops.date_confidence: The name is reported across the Arabic-derived tradition and cited to Ibn Idhari, writing in the 13th century. The sentence usually quoted as his is in fact Wikipedia's own prose, and no translated edition containing it was located; it is given here as unquoted fact. The date is a placeholder for 'later Muslim historiography'.
stops.campa: The Arabic tradition gives the field the name the field itself never had: balat al-shuhada, the pavement of the martyrs, and holds that al-Ghafiqi and many of his men found martyrdom on it. Ibn Idhari carries the name in the thirteenth century, five hundred years after. Henry Coppee points out that the same honorific was given to Toulouse, and to other fields where Muslim armies were beaten, which makes it a formula rather than a marker. It names a defeat, and it can be moved to any defeat that needs it.
suggested_refs: Ibn Idhari al-Marrakushi, al-Bayan al-Mughrib fi Akhbar al-Maghrib, on balat al-shuhada
sources: Henry Coppee, cited in English Wikipedia, 'Battle of Tours'

stops.name: Martel in the Lot, the town that took the name
stops.date_confidence: The town's claim to Charles Martel as founder is undocumented before the 12th century, with the earliest reachable mention around 1142 and the founding legend attested in 16th-century form. The date shown is that earliest mention, not a founding.
stops.campa: A day's ride from Louchapt stands a town called Martel, which holds that Charles Martel founded it in thanksgiving for the victory and put three hammers in its arms to say so. Nothing documents the town before the twelfth century and the founding story is written down later still. The two legends of this country lean on each other: the cliff where the Saracen died, the town the hammer built. Neither needs the other to be true, and neither has ever been asked to be.
suggested_refs: The three hammers in the arms of Martel, Lot, and the Charles Martel founding legend

stops.name: Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, the sword behind the altar
stops.date_confidence: The 1429 recovery of the sword is attested in the trial record. That Charles Martel buried his own sword there as a votive for the victory of 732 is legend, and is the reason the chapel had a sword in it to find.
stops.campa: Charles Martel is said to have buried his sword behind the altar of the chapel at Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, a votive for the defeat of al-Ghafiqi. Seven hundred years later a girl who has never been inside the building sends from Tours and asks the clergy to dig behind that altar for a sword marked with five crosses, and the armourers dig, and there is one. Jeanne d'Arc carries it to Orleans. The chain runs from a dead Umayyad governor in Poitou to a chapel floor to the siege of Orleans, and every link in it is a legend except the sword.
suggested_refs: The chapel of Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois and the sword of the five crosses

stops.name: Moussais, la Fosse au roi
stops.date_confidence: Folk toponymic legend with no archaeological or documentary confirmation located. The date is a placeholder; the tradition is undated and reaches this dossier only through web-search summaries of regional heritage material.
stops.campa: At Moussais a pit in the ground is called la Fosse au roi, the King's Ditch, and is said to hold him. It is the same mistake the Chronicle of 754 made, kept alive in a field name for a thousand years: he was a governor and the Latin west called him a king, and the country where he fell has gone on calling him one. No surviving source names his grave. The French regional histories say it plainly, that the exact place of his burial is unknown, and then the field name says otherwise.
suggested_refs: La Fosse au roi at Moussais, a burial legend without archaeology
sources: French regional heritage tradition, via web search

stops.name: Paris, the bronze in the Louvre
stops.date_confidence: attested; Theodore Gechter's bronze of the combat is dated 1833, Charles de Steuben's history painting of the battle 1837
stops.campa: Theodore Gechter casts the two of them in bronze in 1833, Charles Martel and Abd al-Rahman locked together on rearing horses, and it enters the Louvre. Charles de Steuben paints the battle four years later. This is the century that decides the field between Poitiers and Tours was where Europe was saved, and it decides it with statuary and salon canvases rather than with chronicles, because the chronicles say almost nothing. The Arab historians, Bernard Lewis notes, present it as a minor skirmish.
stops.quote: he slew in that battle 300,000 men, likewise their king by name Abderrahman
stops.quote_source: Chronicle of St. Denis, Account 3 on the Fordham Medieval Sourcebook page 'Arabs, Franks, and the Battle of Tours, 732'; the casualty figure is a chronicle fantasy and the title 'king' is an error for wali
suggested_refs: Theodore Gechter, Combat de Charles Martel et d'Abderame, bronze, 1833, Musee du Louvre

stops.name: Moussais-la-Bataille, the field the visitors come to
stops.date_confidence: attested; more than 40,000 visitors in 2010, ninth most-visited site in the Vienne department, per French Wikipedia. The renaming of the hamlet is attested without a date.
stops.campa: The hamlet is renamed Moussais-la-Bataille and given interpretive panels, and in 2010 more than forty thousand people come to stand on it, which makes it the ninth most-visited site in the Vienne. The scholarship that has grown up beside the panels counts thirty-eight candidate battlefields and will not say which one is right, nor whether the year was 732 or 733, nor whether the day was the tenth of October or the twenty-fifth. Forty thousand people a year come to look at a field that may not be the field.
suggested_refs: The Moussais-la-Bataille heritage site at Vouneuil-sur-Vienne
